hints: Differentiate the velocity function to find acceleration: $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = -0.3t^2 + 3.6t - 6$.
Set $a = 0$ and divide by $-0.3$ to get $t^2 - 12t + 20 = 0$.
walkthrough:
Differentiate velocity with respect to time to find the acceleration function:
$$a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(-0.1t^3 + 1.8t^2 - 6t + 5.6\right) = -0.3t^2 + 3.6t - 6$$

Since $p < q$, identify the roots:
$$p = 2,\quad q = 10$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Relate acceleration to velocity using calculus: acceleration is the first derivative of velocity with respect to time:
$$a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt}$$

Set the acceleration to zero to find the stationary points of velocity:
$$-0.3t^2 + 3.6t - 6 = 0$$

This yields solutions $t = 2$ and $t = 10$. Since $p < q$:
$$p = 2,\quad q = 10$$

hints: Substitute $t = 2$ and $t = 10$ into $v(t)$ to calculate $v(2) = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $v(10) = 25.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Recognize that $t = 2$ is a minimum turning point on the $t$-axis and $t = 10$ is a maximum turning point.
Note that the curve touches the axis at $t = 2$, reaches peak $25.6$ at $t = 10$, crosses the axis at $t = 14$, and is negative from $t = 14$ to $t = 15$.
walkthrough:
Graph characteristics for $0 \leq t \leq 15$:
$$\text{Starts at } (0, 5.6)$$
$$\text{Touches the } t\text{-axis at a smooth local minimum at } (2, 0)$$
$$\text{Rises to a smooth local maximum at } (10, 25.6)$$
$$\text{Crosses the } t\text{-axis at } t = 14\text{ and continues into negative velocity at } t = 15$$
teacher_walkthrough: The curve starts at $(0, 5.6)$ on the vertical axis.
It decreases smoothly to touch the $t$-axis at a local minimum at $(2, 0)$ without crossing it (since $(t-2)^2$ is a double root).
It rises to a smooth local maximum peak of $25.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 10\text{ s}$.
It decreases, crossing the $t$-axis downwards at $t = 14\text{ s}$, and ends below the axis at $(15, -16.9)$.

hints: Notice from the graph that $v(t) \geq 0$ for $0 \leq t \leq 14$, but becomes negative for $14 < t \leq 15$.
To find total distance, split the integration at $t = 14$: $\text{Distance} = \int_0^{14} v\,dt + \left|\int_{14}^{15} v\,dt\right|$.
walkthrough: Identify that velocity changes sign at $t = 14\text{ s}$, being non-negative on $[0, 14]$ and negative on $[14, 15]$.

Integrate the velocity function to obtain the displacement function $F(t)$:
$$F(t) = \int (-0.1t^3 + 1.8t^2 - 6t + 5.6)\,dt = -0.025t^4 + 0.6t^3 - 3t^2 + 5.6t$$

Evaluate the distance for the positive velocity interval $[0, 14]$:
$$d_1 = F(14) - F(0) = 176.4\text{ m}$$

Evaluate the distance for the negative velocity interval $[14, 15]$:
$$d_2 = |F(15) - F(14)| = |168.375 - 176.4| = |-8.025| = 8.025\text{ m}$$

Sum the distances to find the total distance:
$$\text{Total distance} = 176.4 + 8.025 = 184.425\text{ m}\quad \left(=\frac{7377}{40}\text{ m}\right)$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Crucial step: recognize the distinction between displacement and total distance. Because the particle reverses direction and has negative velocity for $t > 14\text{ s}$, the integral must be split at $t = 14\text{ s}$:
$$\text{Total distance} = \int_0^{14} v(t)\,dt + \left|\int_{14}^{15} v(t)\,dt\right|$$

Find the antiderivative $F(t)$ by integrating term-by-term:
$$F(t) = -\frac{0.1}{4}t^4 + \frac{1.8}{3}t^3 - \frac{6}{2}t^2 + 5.6t$$
$$F(t) = -0.025t^4 + 0.6t^3 - 3t^2 + 5.6t$$

Add the two distances to obtain total distance:
$$\text{Total distance} = 176.4 + 8.025 = 184.425\text{ m}\quad \left(=\frac{7377}{40}\text{ m}\right)$$
